advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add `--full-history` (and `--no-merges`/`--no-renames`) to the `git log --diff-filter=D` walk in `_deleted_history` to match the documented flags of `build_ticket_position_commit_map`, or justify why deletion simplification is safe here.
evidence: authorship.py:311-319 reference helper uses `--diff-filter=A`, `--full-history`, `--no-merges`, `--no-renames` and states `--full-history` is 'LOAD BEARING and is NOT dropped ... Without it the answer is topology-dependent and can miss the real introducing commit'
fsck_repair.py:630-635 docstring claims it is 'Modelled on build_ticket_position_commit_map' but only replicates the diff-filter/direction, not the simplification flags
advisory.finding: `_deleted_history` runs `git log --diff-filter=D --name-only` WITHOUT `--full-history` (and without `--no-merges`), but the helper it is explicitly modelled on (`build_ticket_position_commit_map`) documents `--full-history` as 'LOAD BEARING ... NOT dropped — it disables history simplification so the walk sees EVERY add ... Without it the answer is topology-dependent and can miss the real introducing commit.' The deletion walk has the same topology exposure: a deletion committed off the first-parent chain can be simplified away, so a recoverable source is never restored and the ticket is wrongly surfaced for human triage.
scenarios: A source file deleted by a compaction commit that landed on a merged (non-first-parent) branch: git history simplification omits it from the D walk, so restore misses it and rebuild refuses a ticket that was in fact recoverable.
advisory.suggested_fix: Pass `--full-history`, `--no-merges`, `--no-renames` to the `run_git(... "log", "--diff-filter=D", ...)` call in `_deleted_history`, mirroring `build_ticket_position_commit_map`.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile `snapshot_missing_sources` (newest-only) with the per-snapshot `missing_sources_finding` trigger so the guard covers every active snapshot that could feed the rebuild.
evidence: fsck_repair.py:500 `snaps = [n for n in names if is_active_event(n) and n.endswith("-SNAPSHOT.json")]` then line 504 opens only `snaps[-1]`
fsck.py:174-180 `_snap_findings` iterates `for snap_name in sorted(... -SNAPSHOT.json ...)` calling `_check_snapshot` per snapshot
fsck.py:290 `out.extend(_missing_sources_finding(ticket_dir, ticket_id, snapshot_filename, source_uuids))` fires per snapshot
advisory.finding: The fail-closed guard (`snapshot_missing_sources`) inspects ONLY the newest active SNAPSHOT (`snaps[-1]`), but the finding that TRIGGERS the repair (`missing_sources_finding` via `_check_snapshot`) is emitted per-snapshot for every active SNAPSHOT. If an OLDER active snapshot cites missing sources while the newest active snapshot is complete, `SNAPSHOT_MISSING_SOURCES` is reported (so `rebuildable=True`), yet `rebuild_with_restore`/`rebuild_source_state` see no missing sources for the newest snapshot, skip restore, and rebuild from a possibly-incomplete log — defeating the guard for that shape.
scenarios: A ticket dir retaining two active SNAPSHOTs where the earlier one cites deleted sources but the newest is complete: guard on newest returns [] and rebuild proceeds without restoring the earlier snapshot's missing sources.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Align the `SNAPSHOT_MISSING_SOURCES` finding wording with its auto-recoverable-then-fail-closed repair behavior.
evidence: fsck_repair.py:527-529 finding text: `... raw log incomplete — NOT auto-rebuildable, human triage required`
fsck_repair.py:582-587 `rebuildable = any(... or "SNAPSHOT_MISSING_SOURCES" in f ...)` — treated as an auto-repair trigger
advisory.finding: The `SNAPSHOT_MISSING_SOURCES` finding text asserts 'NOT auto-rebuildable, human triage required', but `repair_or_plan` includes `SNAPSHOT_MISSING_SOURCES` in the rebuildable trigger set and will auto restore-then-rebuild it under `--repair`. The user-facing finding contradicts the actual repair behavior when restore succeeds.
scenarios: Operator sees SNAPSHOT_MISSING_SOURCES labelled 'human triage required' on a bare fsck, then `--repair` silently auto-fixes it, undermining trust in the diagnostic wording.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a test that seeds a legacy-compacted closed ticket whose deleted source IS committed in git history, runs rebuild_with_restore (or `fsck --repair-snapshots` mutating), and asserts the ticket reads `closed` again after rebuild.
evidence: search for `rebuild_with_restore` under tests/ returns `(no matches)`

test_restore_recovers_a_source_deleted_by_legacy_compaction (line 203) asserts only that the .retired file exists and snapshot_missing_sources becomes [], but never calls rebuild_with_restore/rebuild afterward nor asserts corrected status

test_rebuild_refuses_when_snapshot_cites_missing_sources (line 87) calls `rebuild_snapshot_from_full_log(...)` directly, not `rebuild_with_restore`, and its deleted_close_uuid was never committed to git, so no restore is attempted
fsck_repair.py:714 `rebuild_with_restore` is the documented "repair path's single entrypoint" yet has no test exercising a successful restore+rebuild
advisory.finding: The central restore-then-rebuild success path (rebuild_with_restore recovers a deleted source from git history, then rebuild_snapshot_from_full_log completes and the reducer re-derives the correct status) is not tested. Tests cover restore_deleted_sources in isolation and the refuse path, but never assert that a ticket whose deleted source is recoverable is rebuilt AND reads its correct (closed) status afterward — the change's primary claim (214/214 returned to correct status).
scenarios: A regression in restore ordering, blob decoding, or the post-restore reduce that leaves the ticket still reverted would not be caught — exactly the b636 failure mode being fixed.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an integration test running `fsck --repair-snapshots` (mutating) against a recoverable legacy ticket and assert the FIXED line is emitted and the finding is resolved on rescan.
evidence: search for `repair_or_plan` under tests/ returns `(no matches)`
the FIXED-line and `resolved` accounting at fsck_repair.py:599-606 have no asserting test
advisory.finding: The mutating repair path repair_or_plan (non-dry-run: rebuild_with_restore success, rescan, resolved count > 0, emitting the "FIXED: rebuilt SNAPSHOT ... after restoring N deleted event(s)" line) is untested. Only the dry-run and read-only branches are exercised, so the actual store-mutating repair introduced by this change has no gating test.
scenarios: A regression in the rescan/resolved-count logic or the FIXED message would go undetected; a repair that fails to resolve findings but reports FIXED would not be caught.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a dry-run test where the missing source IS present in git history and assert the plan line reports 'would restore ... then rebuild'.
evidence: _dry_run_plan branches at fsck_repair.py:615 (`len(candidates) >= len(absent)` => "would restore ... then rebuild") vs line 620 ("would SKIP")

test_repair_snapshots_dry_run_writes_nothing uses `_legacy_compacted_closed_ticket` whose deleted_close_uuid (line 50) is never written to disk or committed, so restore_deleted_sources(dry_run=True) finds no candidate and only the SKIP branch executes
assertion at line 119 only checks `"DRY-RUN" in res.stdout`, not which plan branch fired
advisory.finding: The dry-run 'would restore N deleted event(s) ... then rebuild' branch of _dry_run_plan is untested; the only dry-run test seeds a fixture whose missing source was never committed to git, so it always hits the 'would SKIP ... not safely rebuildable' branch.
scenarios: A regression in the recoverable-count comparison that mislabels a recoverable ticket as unrecoverable (or vice versa) in the dry-run preview would not be caught.
